blocks.en: French has many tenses, but up to B1 eight are enough. The key point is that French has **two pasts side by side** (*passé composé* and *imparfait*) and **two futures**.

children.label: *plus-que-parfait*: *j'avais mangé*
children.en: the pluperfect, it happened even before another past event (B1)

children.label: *imparfait*: *je mangeais*
children.en: description, habit, ongoing action: what it was like

children.label: *futur proche*: *je vais manger*
children.en: plans and the near, certain future

children.label: *futur simple*: *je mangerai*
children.en: the future in general, promises, predictions

items.label: Moods
items.en: they do not say when, but how you look at the action

children.label: *subjonctif*: *que je mange*
children.en: after *il faut que*, wishes and feelings (B1)

items.note: A single finished event: *passé composé*.

items.en: When I was little I used to watch cartoons.
items.fr: Quand j'[[étais]] petit, je [[regardais]] des dessins animés.
items.note: Description and habit in the past: *imparfait*.

blocks.en: You will see the *passé simple* (*il mangea*) in fairy tales and novels instead of the passé composé. You only need to recognise it, not form it. In the verb tables it is marked *literary*.

items.en: I'm going to play basketball. (futur proche)

blocks.en: The *présent* is the most common tense. It corresponds to the English simple and continuous present and is used in much the same way.
When something **has lasted from the past until now**, French uses the *présent* + *depuis*, where English says "I have lived here for three years".

items.en: I've been playing basketball for five years.
items.wrong: J'ai joué au basket depuis cinq ans.
items.note: You are still playing, so the present tense.

blocks.en: To stress that something is happening **right now**: *être en train de* + infinitive. *Je suis en train de manger.* (I'm in the middle of eating.)

items.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? Je lis.
items.en: What are you doing? I'm reading.

items.fr: Le samedi, je joue au basket.
Elle est en train de téléphoner.
items.en: She's on the phone right now.

checks.fr: Je ___ au basket depuis cinq ans.
checks.en: I've been playing basketball for five years.
I've lived here for three years.

a: Je suis en train de manger.

articles.title: What the present tense can do

blocks.en: One French present tense covers **three English ones** (*I eat, I am eating, I do eat*) and more. It also replaces other tenses in many cases. The main uses: **now, habit, general truth, near future, recent past, story telling**.

head: use
example
English
rows: Hier, je sors et je vois Paul.
Yesterday I go out and I see Paul.
On coupe les oignons, on les fait cuire.

blocks.en: For a **planned or sure** future the present is common, especially with a time word: *Demain, je vais au cinéma.* After **si** (if) the present is used for a future condition: *Si tu viens, je suis content.* After **quand** use the futur simple, not the present.

items.fr: Mon train part à huit heures.
Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
items.en: What are you doing this weekend?

items.fr: Si tu veux, on y va.

blocks.en: An action that **started in the past and still goes on** takes the **present** with **depuis** (not the passé composé): *J'apprends le français depuis un an.* (= I have been learning French for a year.)

items.en: I've lived here for three years.
items.wrong: J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans.

items.en: I've been waiting for an hour.

sections.title: Present of the verb être / avoir with age and feelings

blocks.en: Many things are said with **avoir** in the present: *J'ai quinze ans, j'ai faim, j'ai froid, j'ai mal.* *Être* is for states: *Je suis fatigué, je suis content.*

items.en: It's been raining since this morning.

items.fr: Quand j'ai faim, je mange un fruit.
items.en: When I'm hungry I eat a fruit.

items.fr: Je viens de finir mes devoirs.

checks.en: I've lived here for three years.
I've been waiting for an hour.
I've been learning French for a year.
It's been raining since this morning.

checks.fr: J'ai habité ici pendant trois ans.

articles.title: Being in the middle of it: être en train de, être sur le point de

blocks.en: French has no *-ing* tense. To stress that you are **right in the middle of** an action say **être en train de + infinitive**: *Je suis en train de manger* (I'm in the middle of eating). It is the progressive form, and it works in the present and the imparfait.

head: position in time
structure
example
rows: Je suis en train de manger.
être sur le point de + inf.
Je suis sur le point de manger.

blocks.en: Use it when the action is **in progress at that moment** and you want to say so: on the phone (*Je suis en train de cuisiner*), when answering *Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?*, or in a story for an action that was going on when something else happened (*J'étais en train de dormir quand le téléphone a sonné*). For a habit or a general state, the plain present is better.

items.en: I was sleeping when you called.
items.wrong: J'étais en train dormir quand tu as appelé.
items.fr: J'étais [[en train de]] dormir quand tu as appelé.

blocks.en: *En train de* works like any other infinitive link: pronouns go **before the infinitive**, negation goes **around *être***. *Je suis en train de le faire.* *Il n'est pas en train de dormir.*

items.fr: Elle est en train de s'habiller.
Ils ne sont pas en train de travailler.
Je suis en train de lui écrire.
Chut ! Le bébé est en train de dormir.
Tu es en train de faire quoi ?
Quand tu as appelé, j'étais en train de prendre une douche.
items.en: When you called I was taking a shower.

items.fr: Il est sur le point de partir.

a: Je suis en train de manger.

checks.en: She's in the middle of cooking.
a: Elle est en train de cuisiner.

checks.en: He was sleeping when I called.
a: Il était en train de dormir quand j'ai appelé.
Je suis sur le point de partir.
Ils ne sont pas en train de travailler.

checks.task_en: Say that you are in the middle of it
a: Je suis en train de prendre une douche.

blocks.en: The imperative has only three persons, *tu, nous, vous*, and **without a pronoun**. The forms are almost the same as in the present tense: *tu regardes → Regarde !, vous regardez → Regardez !*
With *-er* verbs (and *aller*) the *tu* form loses the ending *-s*: *tu regardes → Regarde !, tu vas → Va !* With other verbs the *-s* stays: *Viens ! Prends ! Finis !*
*Être, avoir, savoir* and *vouloir* have special forms. You will see *veuillez* in polite instructions: *Veuillez patienter.* (Please wait.)
*Aller* in the present tense + an infinitive. The simplest future tense: all you need is *aller*.

rows.en: We're going to eat at noon.

blocks.en: For **plans and things that will happen soon or are certain**. In speech it is much more common than the *futur simple*.

items.note: It is already clear.

blocks.en: Negation wraps around *aller*, pronouns go before the infinitive.

rows.en: I'm not going to go out.
He's going to go to bed.

items.note: After *aller* there is always an infinitive.

items.fr: Ce soir, je vais regarder un film.
items.en: Tonight I'm going to watch a film.

items.fr: Tu vas venir à la fête ?
items.en: Are you going to come to the party?

blocks.en: *Venir* in the present tense + *de* + an infinitive says that something **has just happened**.
Before a vowel *de* shortens: *je viens d'arriver*. With reflexive verbs: *je viens de me lever*.

items.note: *Venir de* + a **place** means "to come from". The meaning "just" exists only with an infinitive.

blocks.en: The *passé composé* is the main past tense of spoken French. It is formed from *avoir* in the present tense + the **past participle**. Most verbs use *avoir*.
For **finished events** in the past: what happened, what you did.
Negation, pronouns and short adverbs all revolve around the **auxiliary**.

items.note: *Être* has its passé composé with *avoir*: *j'ai été*. But "I went, I travelled" is *je suis allé*.

blocks.en: About 15 verbs (mainly of movement) and all reflexive verbs use *être* instead of *avoir*.

items.fr: J'ai regardé un film hier soir.
items.en: I watched a film last night.

items.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait le week-end dernier ?
items.en: What did you do last weekend?

a: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier ?

blocks.en: Regular verbs form the participle from the ending of the infinitive. The irregular ones you have to learn, but there are few and they keep coming back.
It helps to group them by their ending: *-is* (*pris, mis*), *-it* (*dit, écrit, fait*), *-u* (*vu, bu, lu, pu, voulu, su, venu*).
*Parlé, parler, parlez* sound the same. When you don't know what to write, replace the verb with *vendre*. If *vendu* fits, write *-é*. If *vendre* fits, write *-er*.

items.en: I ate it. / I want to eat.
items.note: *J'ai vendu* → *mangé*. *Je veux vendre* → *manger*.

checks.en: I want to eat a pizza.

blocks.en: About 15 verbs and **all reflexive verbs** form the passé composé with *être*. The participle then **agrees with the subject** like an adjective: *+e* for feminine, *+s* for plural.
Mostly movement from place to place or a change of state. They are easy to learn as pairs of opposites:

head: verb
English
participle
rows: to go up, to go down
to become, to come back, to go home, to return

blocks.title: The house of être
blocks.en: Picture a house (*la maison d'être*): someone is born in it, arrives, enters, goes up, falls, comes down, goes out, leaves and dies. Plus all reflexive verbs: *je me suis levé*.

items.fr: Nous sommes restés à la maison.
Tu t'es couché à quelle heure ?
items.en: What time did you go to bed?

checks.task_en: Turn into the passé composé (Léa is speaking)
a: Je suis partie à huit heures.

head: auxiliary
agreement
example
rows: only with a direct object that comes **before** the verb

blocks.en: The participle behaves like an adjective and follows the subject.
With *vous* it depends on whom you mean: *Madame, vous êtes arrivée ?* (one woman), *Les enfants, vous êtes arrivés ?*
With *avoir* the participle **does not change**. The only exception: the direct object (*le, la, les, que*) stands **before** the participle. Then the participle agrees with it.

items.note: The object comes after the participle, so no agreement.
*L'* (Marie) comes before: *vue*.
*Que* stands for *les photos* (feminine plural).

blocks.en: Most of the time you can't hear the agreement (*vu* and *vue* sound the same). You hear it only with participles ending in a consonant: *pris → prise, fait → faite, mis → mise*.

checks.fr: Les photos que j'ai ___ sont belles.
checks.en: The photos I took are beautiful.

blocks.en: The *imparfait* describes the past: **what it was like, what used to be done, what was going on**. In English it often corresponds to "was doing" or "used to do".
Formation: take the *nous* form of the present tense, cut off *-ons* and add *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*.
Only *être* is irregular: the stem *ét-* (*j'étais, nous étions*). With *-ger* and *-cer* the spelling change stays: *je mangeais, je commençais*.

head: use
example
English
rows: Il faisait beau. La maison était grande.
The weather was nice. The house was big.
Le samedi, je jouais au foot.
On Saturdays I used to play football.
Je dormais quand tu as appelé.
I was sleeping when you called.
I was afraid. I was tired.

blocks.en: *Je jouais, tu jouais, il jouait, ils jouaient* all sound the same. Only *-ions* and *-iez* are audible.

items.fr: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Prague.
items.en: When I was little I lived in Prague.

items.fr: Avant, je ne mangeais pas de poisson.
items.en: I didn't use to eat fish.

checks.fr: Quand j'___ petit, j'aimais les dinosaures.
checks.en: When I was little I liked dinosaurs.

checks.fr: Je joue au foot le samedi.
a: Je jouais au foot le samedi.

blocks.en: Think of a film. The *imparfait* is the **scenery**: what the weather was like, what everyone was doing, how everyone felt. The *passé composé* are the **events**: what suddenly happened and moved the story on.

items.en: It was raining when I left the house.
items.note: It was raining (scenery) → *imparfait*. I left (event) → *passé composé*.

items.label: Are you describing what it was like? (weather, looks, feelings, age)
Did it happen repeatedly, as a habit?
Was it going on when something else happened?
items.en: → *imparfait* for the ongoing action: *Je lisais quand...*

items.label: Did it happen once, at a specific moment?
Is it one of a series of events in a row?
items.en: → *passé composé*: *Je me suis levé, j'ai mangé et je suis parti.*

items.label: Does it have a clearly limited duration?
items.en: → *passé composé*: *J'ai habité deux ans à Paris.*

blocks.en: Signal words help, but it is the **meaning** that decides: scenery or event?

sections.title: A rule of thumb for English speakers

blocks.en: Where English says "was doing" or "used to do", French usually wants the *imparfait*. Where English says "did" (one finished action), French usually wants the *passé composé*. It does not always hold, but it is a good first guess.

items.en: I was playing basketball when the phone rang.
items.fr: Je [[jouais]] au basket quand le téléphone [[a sonné]].
Quand je suis arrivé, tout le monde dormait.
items.en: When I arrived, everyone was asleep.

items.fr: Il faisait beau, alors nous sommes allés à la plage.
items.en: The weather was nice, so we went to the beach.

items.fr: Avant, j'allais au collège à pied. Hier, j'ai pris le bus.
items.en: I used to walk to school. Yesterday I took the bus.

items.fr: J'avais faim, donc j'ai mangé une pomme.
items.en: I was hungry, so I ate an apple.

checks.fr: Je regardais la télé quand mon père ___ arrivé.
checks.en: I was watching TV when my father arrived.

checks.fr: Quand j'étais petit, je ___ au foot tous les jours.
checks.en: When I was little I played football every day.
The weather was nice, so we went out.
a: Il faisait beau, {alors|donc} nous sommes sortis.
Il faisait beau, {alors|donc} on est sortis.

blocks.en: *Futur simple* = infinitive + the endings *-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont* (they sound like the present tense of *avoir*). With verbs in *-re* the final *-e* is dropped: *prendre → je prendrai*.
The endings are always the same, only the stem changes. The most common:
The giveaway of the future: you can always hear an *r* before the ending.

head: futur proche
futur simple
rows: spoken language, plans, the near future
written text, promises, predictions, the distant future

blocks.en: You can often use either. After *quand* about the future and in the main clause after *si*, the *futur simple* is used.

items.en: Tomorrow the weather will be nice.

items.fr: Quand je serai grand, je serai pilote.
items.en: When I'm big I'll be a pilot.

items.fr: Nous irons en France l'été prochain.
items.en: We'll go to France next summer.

checks.en: Tomorrow we'll go to the cinema.
Will you do your homework later?

articles.title: Futur antérieur: what will have happened

blocks.en: The **futur antérieur** is the **future perfect**: *j'aurai fini* = I will have finished. It is **avoir or être in the futur simple + the past participle**, with the same auxiliaries and agreement rules as the passé composé.

1) An action that will be **finished before another future action**: *Quand j'aurai fini, je sortirai.* 2) After **quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, une fois que, après que** when the main verb is in the future. 3) A **supposition about the past**: *Il n'est pas là, il aura oublié.* (He probably forgot.)

items.fr: Dès que j'aurai fini, je t'appellerai.
items.en: As soon as I've finished I'll call you.

items.fr: Quand elle sera arrivée, nous mangerons.
items.en: When she has arrived we'll eat.
He must have forgotten our appointment.

blocks.en: Both clauses in the future and **one finished before the other**: first action in the *futur antérieur*, the second in the *futur simple*. If the two actions happen at the same time use *futur simple* twice.

items.en: When I've finished, I'll go out.
items.note: The first action is finished first.
Same time: both futur simple.

items.fr: Demain à cette heure-ci, j'aurai fini mon examen.
items.en: Tomorrow at this time I'll have finished my exam.

items.fr: Lorsque tu auras lu ce livre, prête-le-moi.
items.en: When you've read this book, lend it to me.

checks.en: As soon as I've finished, I'll call you.
a: Dès que j'aurai fini, je t'appellerai.

checks.en: When she has arrived, we'll eat.
a: Quand elle sera arrivée, nous mangerons.
Quand elle sera arrivée, on mangera.

checks.en: When I've finished, I'll go out.
As soon as she's home, we'll have dinner.

checks.task_en: Put the first verb in the futur antérieur

blocks.en: The *conditionnel* corresponds to English "would". It is formed from the **stem of the futur simple** + the **endings of the imparfait** *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*: *je jouerai* (I will play) → *je jouerais* (I would play).

head: use
example
English
rows: I would like to go to Japan.
Si j'avais le temps, je viendrais.
If I had time, I would come.

items.en: If I were rich, I would buy a car.
items.wrong: Si je serais riche, j'achèterais une voiture.
items.fr: Si j'[[étais]] riche, j'achèterais une voiture.
items.note: Never the conditionnel after *si*, but the *imparfait*.

blocks.en: *Je jouerai* (I will play) and *je jouerais* (I would play) sound almost the same. In writing the single *-s* decides.

items.fr: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
items.en: I would like a croissant, please.

items.fr: À ta place, je ne ferais pas ça.
items.en: If I were you, I wouldn't do that.
We could go to the cinema.

checks.fr: Je ___ un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
checks.en: I would like a glass of water, please.

blocks.en: The *plus-que-parfait* expresses an action that happened **even before another past action**. It is formed like the passé composé, only the auxiliary is in the *imparfait*: *j'avais mangé, j'étais parti*.
English says "had done", sometimes just "already" or "before". French changes the tense.

items.en: When I arrived, the film had already started.
items.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, le film [[avait]] déjà [[commencé]].
items.note: The film started before I arrived.

items.en: I wasn't hungry because I had eaten.
items.fr: Je n'avais pas faim parce que j'[[avais mangé]].

sections.title: Rules as for the passé composé

blocks.en: The choice of *avoir* and *être*, participle agreement and the place of negation work the same as in the passé composé: *Elle était déjà partie. Je n'avais pas compris.*

items.fr: Il avait plu toute la nuit.
Elle était déjà partie quand je suis arrivé.
items.en: She had already left when I arrived.

items.fr: Nous n'avions jamais vu la mer.
items.en: We had never seen the sea.

checks.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, le film ___ déjà commencé.
checks.en: When I arrived, the film had already started.

articles.title: Which tense goes with which: sequence of tenses

blocks.en: In French the tense of the **second clause depends on the tense of the first**. Past + past: the second clause often moves **one step back** (reported speech, *si* clauses, backgrounds). The table gives the common pairs.

head: main clause
dependent clause
example
rows: Je pense qu'il vient / viendra / est venu.
Il a dit qu'il était malade.
Il a dit qu'il avait mangé.
Si tu étais venu, je serais parti.

blocks.en: When the reporting verb is in the **past**, the verb of the reported statement shifts: **présent → imparfait**, **passé composé → plus-que-parfait**, **futur → conditionnel**, **futur proche → *allait* + infinitive**. Time words shift as well: *demain → le lendemain*, *hier → la veille*, *maintenant → à ce moment-là*, *ici → là*.

items.fr: « Je suis fatigué. » → Il a dit qu'il était fatigué.
« J'ai fini. » → Elle a dit qu'elle avait fini.
« Je viendrai demain. » → Il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain.
items.en: He said he'd come the next day.

blocks.en: In a story the **background** (description, habits, states) is in the **imparfait**, the **main events** are in the **passé composé**, and **what had happened before** is in the **plus-que-parfait**. See the article about passé composé and imparfait.

items.en: It was raining. We went home.

items.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient déjà partis.
items.en: When I arrived they had already left.

items.fr: Elle avait faim parce qu'elle n'avait rien mangé.
items.en: She was hungry because she hadn't eaten anything.

items.wrong: Il a dit qu'il est fatigué.

items.fr: Elle m'a dit qu'elle habitait à Lyon.
items.en: She told me she lived in Lyon.

items.fr: Je ne savais pas qu'il avait déjà mangé.
items.en: I didn't know he had already eaten.
He promised he would call me.

items.fr: Si j'avais de l'argent, j'achèterais un vélo.
items.en: If I had money I would buy a bike.

a: Il a dit qu'il était fatigué.
Elle a dit qu'elle avait fini.
Il a dit qu'il était malade.

checks.en: She told me she had already eaten.
a: Elle m'a dit qu'elle avait déjà mangé.

checks.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, ils ___ déjà partis.
checks.en: When I arrived they had already left.

checks.fr: Si j'___ de l'argent, j'achèterais un vélo.
checks.en: If I had money I'd buy a bike.

head: type
clause with si
main clause
example
rows: Si j'avais le temps, je jouerais.

blocks.en: The golden rule: **never a future or a conditional after *si***.
If something happens (and it may well happen), what follows from it.

items.fr: S'il pleut, je reste à la maison.
items.en: If it rains, I stay at home.

blocks.en: If it were so (but it isn't): *si* + *imparfait*, and the main clause in the *conditionnel*.

rows.en: If I were rich, I would buy a house.

items.en: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home.
items.wrong: S'il pleuvra demain, je resterai à la maison.
items.fr: S'il [[pleut]] demain, je resterai à la maison.
items.note: As in English ("if it rains"), *si* takes the present tense, never the future.

items.en: If I knew, I would tell you.
items.wrong: Si je saurais, je te le dirais.
items.fr: Si je [[savais]], je te le dirais.

blocks.en: *Si + il* = *s'il*, *si + ils* = *s'ils*. But *si elle, si on* is not shortened.

items.fr: Si on gagne, on fera la fête.
items.en: If we win, we'll have a party.

items.fr: Si j'étais toi, je ne ferais pas ça.

items.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu ferais si tu gagnais au loto ?

checks.en: If you come tomorrow, we'll go to the park.

checks.en: If I were rich, I would buy a car.

checks.fr: S'il ___ demain, je resterai à la maison.
checks.en: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home.
If I had a dog, I would be happy.
a: Si j'avais un chien, je serais {heureux|heureuse|content|contente}.

articles.title: Conditionnel passé: j'aurais dû, il aurait fallu

blocks.en: The **conditionnel passé** is **avoir or être in the conditionnel présent + the past participle**: *j'aurais mangé, elle serait partie*. It means **would have** and is used for **regrets, reproaches and unreal past situations**.

head: use
example
English
rows: Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
If I'd known I would have come.
I would have liked to talk to you.
There are said to be ten injured.

blocks.en: The **unreal past** has the pattern: **si + plus-que-parfait**, **conditionnel passé**. The condition did not happen and so neither did the result. Never put the conditional after *si*.

items.en: If I had known, I would have come.
items.wrong: Si j'aurais su, je serais venu.
items.note: No conditional after *si*.

items.en: If you had come earlier, you would have seen him.
items.wrong: Si tu viendrais plus tôt, tu l'aurais vu.
items.fr: Si tu [[étais venu]] plus tôt, tu l'[[aurais vu]].

blocks.en: *J'aurais dû* (I should have) and *j'aurais pu* (I could have) are the most frequent forms. They are followed by the **infinitive**: *J'aurais dû partir plus tôt.*

items.fr: Tu aurais dû me le dire.

items.en: She would have liked to stay.

items.fr: Si j'avais eu le temps, j'aurais voyagé.
items.en: If I'd had time I would have travelled.

items.fr: Il aurait mieux valu rester à la maison.
items.en: It would have been better to stay home.

items.fr: À ta place, je n'aurais rien dit.
items.en: In your place I wouldn't have said anything.

items.fr: Elle serait venue si elle avait été libre.
items.en: She would have come if she'd been free.

blocks.en: The *subjonctif* is a mood used **after *que*** following expressions of necessity, wishes and feelings. Up to B1 you only need its present tense and a handful of expressions that trigger it.
Take the *ils* form of the present tense, cut off *-ent* and add *-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent*. With *-er* verbs it looks almost the same as the present tense.

head: expression
meaning
example
rows: it is necessary that / you must
Je parle lentement pour que tu comprennes.
Bien qu'il soit malade, il joue.
Je suis content que tu sois là.

blocks.en: When the subject is the same in both parts, an infinitive is used: *Je veux partir* (I want to leave), not *je veux que je parte*.

items.note: After *je pense que* there is an ordinary indicative. The subjonctif comes only after the negative *je ne pense pas que*.

blocks.en: The subjunctive is used in a **que-clause when the speaker's attitude comes first**: a **wish, an order, a feeling, a doubt, a judgement**. It is **not** used for facts you simply state. It also needs a **different subject** in the two parts; with the same subject French uses the **infinitive**.

head: after
example
English
rows: wish, will: vouloir, souhaiter, préférer, exiger, demander que
necessity: il faut que, il est nécessaire que
feeling: être content que, avoir peur que, regretter que
Je suis content que tu sois là.
doubt: douter que, il est possible que, il se peut que
judgement: il est important que, c'est dommage que
negative opinion: ne pas penser que, ne pas croire que
Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne.
I don't think he is coming.

blocks.en: After verbs of **certainty and knowledge** (*penser que, croire que, savoir que, espérer que, il est certain que, il est vrai que, je trouve que*) in the affirmative use the **indicative**. After the **same verbs in the negative or in a question** with doubt use the subjunctive. *Espérer que* always takes the indicative.

items.wrong: Je ne pense pas qu'il vient.

items.note: Always indicative; the future is common.

sections.title: Infinitive when the subject is the same

blocks.en: When the **subject does not change** use **verb + de + infinitive** or the verb alone, not a *que*-clause: *Je veux partir* (not *Je veux que je parte*). *Je suis content de venir.* *Il faut partir* (general) or *il faut que je parte* (I).

items.wrong: Je suis content que je suis là.

blocks.en: The present subjunctive is in the article about the subjunctive basics. The most important irregulars are *être* (**sois**), *avoir* (**aie**), *aller* (**aille**), *faire* (**fasse**), *pouvoir* (**puisse**), *savoir* (**sache**), *vouloir* (**veuille**).

articles.title: Conjunctions with the subjunctive: pour que, bien que, avant que

blocks.en: Some conjunctions **always** take the subjunctive, others **always** take the indicative. Learn them as two lists. If both clauses have the **same subject**, use a preposition + infinitive instead (*avant de, pour, sans, à condition de*).

items.fr: Je te prête mon livre à condition que tu me le rendes.
items.en: I'll lend you my book provided that you give it back.

items.fr: Il est sorti sans que personne le voie.
items.en: He went out without anyone seeing him.

items.fr: Reste ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
items.en: Stay here until I come back.

items.fr: Je ne sortirai pas à moins qu'il fasse beau.
items.en: I won't go out unless the weather is fine.

blocks.en: **Après que** is followed by the **indicative** (the action is already a fact): *Après qu'il est parti, j'ai pleuré.* Many French speakers wrongly use the subjunctive, but the indicative is the rule.

With the same subject: *avant de partir, pour réussir, sans dire, à condition de venir*. With different subjects: *avant que tu partes, pour que je réussisse, sans que tu dises, à condition que tu viennes*.

blocks.en: The *gérondif* is *en* + a form in *-ant*. It says that two things happen **at the same time**, or **how** something is done. The subject must be the same for both actions.
Take the *nous* form of the present tense and replace *-ons* with *-ant*: *nous faisons → en faisant*.
Exceptions: *être → en étant, avoir → en ayant, savoir → en sachant*.
